title: GAE: Generalizable Action Expert for Robot Control
one_liner: A robot learns to move smoothly by first mastering motion from trajectories alone, then adding a 3D position corrector trained on point clouds.
lead: Vision-language models can reason about tasks — they predict where a robot's end should go — but converting that reasoning into smooth, accurate robot motion is hard. This paper splits the problem in two stages: first learn how to move smoothly from a huge dataset of pure motion trajectories, then fine-tune a separate 3D position corrector to understand what the camera sees. This separation is faster to train because each stage does one focused job, and it works on new scenes because the smooth-motion core stays unchanged.

problem.h2: Why robots cannot simply follow a language command
paras: A language model can read 'stack the blue cup on the red one' and reason about which cup to grab and where to place it. But a robot needs precise, continuous motion commands — tiny adjustments to every joint every fraction of a second. If you train one system to do both reasoning and motion together, two things go wrong: the system becomes too tangled to reuse on new tasks, and it needs expensive data from every specific robot and every specific camera angle.

Teams have tried training a single end-to-end system: take the image, reason about the task, output the motion — all at once. This works in the lab, but fails badly when the camera moves, the lighting changes, or the robot sits in a new building.

callout.html: Learn motion control from motion data alone, then attach a separate 3D position corrector that reads the point cloud and maps predicted positions to actual objects.

steps.b: Step 1: Stage one — pretraining on motion
steps.text: Feed the action expert pure trajectory data (150,000 examples from robots), with point cloud features masked out. It learns to turn waypoints into smooth, continuous motion.

steps.b: Step 2: Stage two — fine-tuning point-cloud corrector
steps.text: Freeze the trained motion expert. Feed it new data with actual point clouds visible. A separate lightweight corrector learns to read the 3D scene and adjust the predicted positions.

steps.b: Step 3: Language model predicts target positions
steps.text: For a new task, the language model reads the image and the command, then outputs a sparse set of 3D coordinates (e.g., 'grasp here, place there').

steps.b: Step 4: Point-cloud corrector grounds the predictions
steps.text: The corrector looks at the real point cloud and adjusts the predicted positions to match actual 3D objects in the scene.
The pre-trained motion expert converts the grounded waypoints into smooth robot commands, and the robot moves.

paras: The paper changes how and when the motion model learns. Instead of training all at once on images and trajectories mixed together, it separates them: pure motion first (pretraining), pure 3D position correction second (fine-tuning).

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: position prediction error
hidden.name: Gap between predicted and actual 3D target locations
paras: When a language model predicts where the robot should go, those predictions come from a 2D image, not from the real 3D space around the robot. The actual robot arm occupies 3D space filled with real obstacles. The paper measures how far the language model's guesses are from the true 3D positions of objects in the scene. This is not a single number you can see; it is the tiny spatial error that accumulates across all the positions the robot must reach.

During stage one (pretraining), the model ignores this error — it only sees trajectories, no point clouds. During stage two, the corrector learns to measure and fix this error. The paper tracks this by testing on held-out point clouds: Can the corrector take a language model's 2D-based predictions and convert them into accurate 3D positions that match what the camera sees?

heat.caption: Darker cells are position errors the corrector learns to fix. Highlighted cells are what the paper directly improves.

reads.html: The language model's 3D guesses are often wrong because it was trained only on 2D images. The corrector learns where things actually are in 3D.
The APPF scheme decouples motion learning from 3D correction, so the corrector trains only on the position-fixing task, not on motion modeling.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the decoupling strategy
paras: Imagine teaching someone to ride a bike versus teaching them to navigate. If you try to teach both at once — 'Learn to steer AND learn to balance AND learn the route' — the student gets confused and none of it sticks. If instead you teach steering and balance first on a quiet road with many repeated paths, then hand them a map, the student learns much faster because the repeated motion patterns are clear and uncluttered, and they can handle new routes because the core skill (balance and steering) is solid.

The paper does the same thing with robots. The motion expert learns from pure trajectories (150,000 examples), where every aspect of smooth movement is clear because there is no visual noise or camera variation. Once this motion expert is solid, it becomes a reusable core that works on any task. Then, a lightweight corrector learns only one narrow job: 'Look at the 3D point cloud, adjust the predicted positions to match what you see, and feed them to the motion expert.' This corrector is simple and trains much faster because it is focused only on reading 3D and correcting positions — not also learning how to move smoothly or balancing different tasks.

The separation also prevents catastrophic forgetting. If the corrector were trained jointly with the motion expert, learning new tasks would slowly degrade the motion expert's smooth-motion skills. By freezing the motion expert and fine-tuning only the corrector, the paper ensures that the core skill (smooth motion) stays sharp across all tasks and scenes, so the robot moves the same way whether it is stacking or grasping or assembling.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Pretraining: On a dataset of 150,000 arm trajectories (no camera data), the motion expert learns: given target positions [t1, t2, t3], output smooth actions. Loss drops from 2.5 to 0.3.

Fine-tuning on one new task: Corrector sees a point cloud, adjusts predicted position 1 from (0.5, 0.3) to (0.52, 0.32) (0.02 meter correction). The frozen motion expert converts that into smooth actions; loss is 0.28.
Frozen motion expert keeps its skill (0.3 → 0.28 is tiny change); corrector does all the heavy lifting. This separation means corrector training is clean and fast.

math.note: Freezing the motion expert during fine-tuning keeps its smooth-motion skill sharp, so the robot moves the same way across all tasks.

charts.title: End-to-end baseline (motion + correction trained together)
charts.note: Training motion and correction at the same time causes the motion skill to degrade on longer sequences, because the corrector's learning interferes with the motion expert's smooth-motion patterns.

charts.title: This paper (APPF: stage-by-stage)
charts.note: Decoupling keeps the motion skill sharp, so longer sequences stay smooth. Correction fine-tuning does not interfere with motion patterns because the motion expert is frozen.

items.html: The point cloud comes from a depth camera that may have errors in shadows or on shiny surfaces. If the corrector is never trained on noisy point clouds, it will fail when deployed on a real robot. The paper assumes clean depth data.

The language model may predict 3D coordinates the robot's arm cannot physically reach. The corrector has no way to fix physical impossibilities. The paper relies on the language model staying within the robot's workspace.

items.b: Pretraining data bias limits motion generalization.
items.html: If the 150,000 pretraining trajectories come from one type of task or one camera angle, the motion expert learns habits specific to that setting. The frozen motion expert will then perform poorly on radically different tasks, because its pretraining biased it toward the old motion style.

items.b: Done right: careful pre-training plus correction-only fine-tuning.
items.html: When the pretraining dataset is diverse (many task types and camera setups) and the corrector is lightweight (trains fast), the decoupling works as intended. The frozen motion expert stays sharp, and correction fine-tuning is efficient.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a minimal robot task: a pick-and-place with three objects. Collect two datasets: (1) 2000 demonstration arm trajectories from simulation, recorded as lists of joint positions over time — this is your pretraining data. (2) 500 multimodal examples (language command, image, point cloud, correct action trajectory) on the real task. Train a motion expert only on dataset (1), then fine-tune only the corrector on dataset (2). Compare success rate to a baseline that trains both jointly on dataset (2) from scratch. The demo should show that decoupling is faster to train because each stage focuses on one job, and it achieves higher success rate on new objects the model never saw because the frozen motion expert does not degrade.
demo.closing: If the motion expert has learned smooth motion, then adding a corrector should be pure upside — no motion degradation, only correction improvement. The metric should be clearly positive.
